How to Make Woven Napkin Rings for Dinner Parties

Make a set of six woven napkin rings in one sitting. Each one takes ten minutes and about 60 cm of palm strip, and the set costs almost nothing.

5 September 2025 ME By Maya Ellis 7 min read 567 words
Share

In short

Make a set of six woven napkin rings in one sitting. Each one takes ten minutes and about 60 cm of palm strip, and the set costs almost nothing.

Napkin rings are the ideal project for a rainy evening before guests arrive. Each one takes about ten minutes and a single 60 cm strip, so a set of six is done in an hour and costs you one leaf.

The trick is sizing. A ring needs an inner diameter of about 4 cm to slip over a rolled linen napkin and grip it without crushing it. Get that measurement right and the weave almost looks after itself.

What makes woven rings worth the effort is that they are genuinely useful, not decorative clutter. They hold a rolled napkin in place, they sit flat on a plate, and they store in a small box between dinners. Because they use so little material, they are also the best project for using up the short offcuts left over from a larger basket.

Sizing and preparing the strips

Cut your strips 60 cm long and 0.8 cm wide. A strip narrower than that is fiddly to hold; wider and the ring looks clumsy on the plate. Soak the strips for five minutes in warm water, then run each one between your thumb and a blunt blade to soften it. You should be able to wrap it around a finger with no cracking.

What You'll Need

  • 6 palm leaf strips, 0.8 cm wide and 60 cm long, one per ring
  • A small cup or tube about 4 cm across to size the ring
  • Sharp scissors
  • Warm water for soaking
  • A peg to hold the first wrap

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. 1

    Soak and soften

    Soak each strip in warm water for five minutes, then draw it between your thumb and a blunt knife until it flexes easily. Damp strips grip each other and hold the weave.

  2. 2

    Wrap the first loop

    Wrap the strip once around your 4 cm cup, leaving a 6 cm tail. Peg the overlap so the loop cannot spring open while you work.

  3. 3

    Weave around

    Pass the long end under the loop, over the top, and back through, repeating around the ring. Keep each wrap tight against the last so no gaps show.

  4. 4

    Cover the join

    When you meet your starting tail, weave the last two wraps over both tails so the join disappears into the pattern rather than sitting on the surface.

  5. 5

    Tuck and trim

    Trim both tails to 2 cm, tuck them under the final wrap, and press the ring gently flat on the table so it sits level on a plate.

Making a matching set

Consistency matters more than perfection here, because six slightly different rings look careless while six identical ones look bought. Cut all six strips to the same length before you start, use the same cup as your form, and count your wraps so each ring has the same number. I aim for eleven wraps per ring.

Helpful Tips

  • Make one extra ring in case one splits while you are learning.
  • Press each ring under a heavy book for an hour after weaving so it dries perfectly round.
  • Store the set in a small box with a little tissue so the rings keep their shape between dinners.
  • Use narrow offcuts from a basket project; you only need 60 cm per ring.

If a ring feels loose on the napkin, re-soak it, wrap it once more around a slightly smaller cup and let it dry in place.

Frequently asked questions

What size should a woven napkin ring be?

An inner diameter of about 4 cm fits most rolled linen napkins. Wrap around a 4 cm cup to size each ring so the whole set matches.

How long does one napkin ring take to make?

About ten minutes once your strips are soaked. A set of six is comfortably an hour, including drying time if you press them flat.

How much palm strip does a napkin ring use?

One strip about 60 cm long and 0.8 cm wide per ring, so a set of six uses roughly 3.6 metres in total.

Will woven napkin rings survive washing?

Keep them away from water. Wipe with a dry cloth only; soaking the rings will soften the weave and they will lose their round shape.
